title: The $27 List Muhammad Yunus Made in Jobra
dek: After the 1974 famine an economics professor listed his neighbours' debts, paid them himself, then spent months persuading a bank to lend to the poor.

story.event: Paying off the $27 owed by 42 villagers in Jobra and becoming guarantor for the first bank loans to the poor
story.summary: In the mid-1970s, after Bangladesh's 1974 famine, the Chittagong University economist Muhammad Yunus found 42 people in the village of Jobra owing moneylenders a total of $27 and paid it from his own pocket. When the campus bank refused to lend to the poor, he became guarantor himself; the Grameen Bank Project began in Jobra in 1976 and became Grameen Bank in 1983. Its repayment rates, above 98 per cent by Grameen's and its supporters' figures, were challenged by a Wall Street Journal report that 19 per cent of loans were overdue.
paragraphs: In 1974 famine spread through Bangladesh, and Muhammad Yunus, who headed the economics department at Chittagong University, found it hard to stand in a classroom teaching what he called "elegant theories of economics." He began walking into Jobra, the village beside the campus, hoping, he later said, to be of use to someone even for a day.

What he found there was debt measured in cents. One woman was borrowing less than a dollar from a moneylender who, in return, could buy everything she made at a price he set. Yunus drew up a list of people in the village caught in loans like hers. It came to 42 names and a total of $27. He paid it from his own pocket and, as he recalled it in 2007, told them to "return the money, be free." Their relief was so plain that he asked himself why he should not do more.

The harder step was persuading a bank. He went to the one on the campus, and the manager refused: a bank could not lend to the poor, whatever the amount. After several months of failed efforts, Yunus offered himself as guarantor and signed for the loans. The manager, he remembered, said: "Say goodbye to your money because it's not going to come back." By Yunus's account the borrowers repaid on time. The project began in Jobra in 1976 and spread to other villages, but growing it through existing banks stayed difficult, and in 1983 he succeeded in creating a separate bank, Grameen Bank.

The figures that followed were mostly Grameen's own. In 1984 the Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation reported that more than 100,000 villagers had borrowed and on-time repayment was above 98 per cent. Accepting the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006, which he shared with the bank, Yunus spoke of nearly 7 million borrowers, 97 per cent of them women, and a repayment rate of 99 per cent. Not everyone accepted the counting: a Wall Street Journal report co-written by Daniel Pearl found 19 per cent of the bank's loans overdue, and Yunus disputed parts of it.

quote.text: trying to get into business and trying to get out of debt, a very ancient slough, called by the Latins æs alienum, another’s brass, for some of their coins were made of brass; still living, and dying, and buried by this other’s brass
quote.source_title: Walden, and On The Duty Of Civil Disobedience, Project Gutenberg eBook #205
quote.connection: Yunus told the 42 to repay him and be free. Thoreau, looking at his own New England neighbours, saw debt itself as a slough people live and die in. Grameen's later arguments over overdue loans suggest his question was never fully answered.

reflection: Yunus's first act took a few days and $27. What took years was the second question: whether an institution could keep doing it without him paying. His answer was to put his own name behind people a bank thought unreliable, before anyone else would.

Thoreau would ask whether swapping one lender for another is freedom at all, and Grameen's overdue loans suggest he had a point. Both can be true: trust can open a door and still leave a weight on the person who walks through it. You do not have to settle that this morning. It is enough to notice where, in your own work, you are already vouching for someone, and whether they know.
invitation: Think of one colleague whose work you would put your own name behind. Tell them so today, in one plain sentence, and say what it is about their work that earns it.

research_notes: Who received the $27: the slate said 42 women. Yunus's own accounts (Nobel lecture 2006, CNN 2007) say 42 'victims' or 'people'; BBC (2011) says 42 women and the Daily Star (2006) says 42 female basket weavers. The story follows Yunus and says 42 people. Gift or loan: the lecture says he 'offered' the money; in the 2007 interview he says he gave it and told them to return it; the Daily Star says he lent it; the story says he paid it and told them to return it. Date: the lecture places the start in the 1974 famine without dating the list; BBC says Yunus dates the idea to 1976, and the Magsaysay Foundation dates the Grameen Bank Project at Jobra to 1976, so the story gives 1974 for the famine and 1976 for the project and does not date the $27 itself. Outcome numbers: Magsaysay 1984, more than 100,000 villagers and better than 98 per cent on-time repayment; Daily Star 2006, 6.5 million people; Nobel lecture 2006, nearly 7.0 million borrowers, 97 per cent women, 99 per cent repayment and an internal survey claiming 58 per cent crossed the poverty line (not used); CNN 2007, 7.3 million. The repayment figures are Grameen's or its supporters'; the Wall Street Journal report by Daniel Pearl and Michael Phillips (dated 27 November 2001 in other references; BBC says 2002) found 19 per cent of loans overdue overall and half the portfolio a year overdue in two northern districts, which Yunus partly disputed. The story gives the claims with who made them and the challenge, and does not date the WSJ report. The bank manager's words and the timing of his guarantee rest on Yunus's own recollection and are attributed. Funding is set to 'mixed' rather than the slate's 'nonprofit': the first $27 was his own money, and the project then ran on state-bank loans he personally guaranteed; Grameen Bank is a borrower-owned bank created by government ordinance. Later events (his removal as managing director in 2011) are outside this episode. Thoreau's passage is about debt among his Concord neighbours; it is applied here by analogy.
